weeks.context: This week you are going to analyze Sample Superstore — the classic dataset every analyst learns on. It's 4 years of sales for a fictional retailer. By Sunday you'll have a 1-page Excel/Sheets dashboard plus a 1-page PDF memo answering 3 specific questions. If you have never used Excel formulas or pivot tables before, that is fine. Every step is shown.

days.title: What does a data analyst do?
days.summary: Watch and think. No spreadsheet today.

items.title: Day in the life of a Data Analyst (12 min)
items.creator: various

items.title: The 3 questions
items.body:
By Sunday you'll answer these about Sample Superstore (a fake retailer):

Q1. Which sub-category (Phones? Chairs? Tables?) has the highest profit MARGIN? Which has the lowest?
Q2. Which region (West? East? Central? South?) grew sales the most year-over-year in the latest year?
Q3. Is Furniture overall a profitable category? Where does its profit come from?

Write your guess for each in guesses.txt. Check on Day 6.

items.title: Sample Superstore — Tableau (free download)
items.why: Click 'Open' to download. If the page asks for a Tableau login, sign up — free. The file is 'Sample - Superstore.xls'.

items.title: Open and explore
items.body:
STEP 1 — Make the project folder.
  Make a folder on your Desktop called 'superstore-analysis'.

STEP 2 — Download the file from the card above. Move it into the folder.

STEP 3 — Open it.
  Right-click → Open with → Excel (or Google Sheets — upload via drive.google.com).

STEP 4 — Look at the sheets.
  YOU SHOULD SEE 3 sheets at the bottom: Orders, Returns, People.
  Click Orders. Scroll through. You see ~10,000 rows. Look at the columns: Order Date, Region, Segment, Category, Sub-Category, Sales, Quantity, Discount, Profit.

STEP 5 — Take a quick total.
  In a new cell anywhere: =SUM(Orders!N:N)
  (N is the Sales column — adjust the letter if yours is different.)
  YOU SHOULD SEE: about $2.3 million in total Sales. That's the size of the dataset.

Save the file. Done for today.

days.title: Practice the 7 essential formulas
days.summary: Today you learn the formulas every analyst uses daily.

items.title: Excel essentials — Leila Gharani (45 min)
items.creator: Leila Gharani
items.why: The best Excel teacher on YouTube.

items.title: Drill the formulas
items.body:
Make a new sheet in the same workbook called 'Drills'.

STEP 1 — In A1 type 'Total sales 2023:', in B1 type:
      =SUMIFS(Orders!N:N, Orders!C:C, ">=2023-01-01", Orders!C:C, "<=2023-12-31")
  (Adjust column letters if yours are different. N=Sales, C=Order Date.)
  YOU SHOULD SEE: ~$700k.

STEP 2 — In A2 type 'Orders in West:', in B2 type:
      =COUNTIFS(Orders!I:I, "West")
  (I = Region column)
  YOU SHOULD SEE: ~3,000 orders.

STEP 3 — In A3 type 'Average discount:', in B3 type:
      =AVERAGE(Orders!O:O)
  (O = Discount)

STEP 4 — In A4 type 'XLOOKUP for customer CG-12520:', in B4 type:
      =XLOOKUP("CG-12520", Orders!E:E, Orders!F:F)
  YOU SHOULD SEE: that customer's name.

STEP 5 — In A5 type 'High-margin orders:', in B5 type a header. Then in row 6+ for the first 100 rows, add a new column 'Margin Bucket' next to Profit. Use:
      =IF(R2/N2 > 0.2, "Healthy", IF(R2/N2 > 0.05, "Thin", "Loss"))
  (R = Profit, N = Sales)

Save.

days.title: Pivot table for Q1 (margin leaders)
days.summary: Pivot tables — the most useful tool an analyst has.

items.title: Pivot tables in 20 minutes — Leila Gharani
items.creator: Leila Gharani

items.title: Build the margin pivot
items.body:
STEP 1 — Click anywhere in the Orders sheet.
  Insert → PivotTable → New worksheet → OK.

STEP 2 — Build the pivot.
  ROWS area: drag Sub-Category
  VALUES area: drag Sales (Sum), drag Profit (Sum)
  You should now see ~17 sub-categories with their Sales and Profit totals.

STEP 3 — Add Margin as a calculated field.
  PivotTable Analyze tab → Fields, Items, & Sets → Calculated Field.
  Name: Margin. Formula: = Profit / Sales
  Click OK.

STEP 4 — Format Margin as a percentage.
  Right-click any Margin number → Number Format → Percentage → 1 decimal → OK.

STEP 5 — Sort by Margin descending.
  Click the dropdown next to 'Sub-Category' → More Sort Options → Sort by Margin → Largest to Smallest.

STEP 6 — Write the answer to Q1.
  In a new cell: highest margin sub-category = ?
  Lowest margin sub-category = ?
  Save.

items.title: Region YoY pivot
items.body:
STEP 1 — New pivot from Orders → new sheet.

STEP 2 — Build it.
  ROWS: Region
  COLUMNS: Order Date — Excel will offer to group by Year. Accept.
  VALUES: Sum of Sales
  You see a 4x4 table: each region's sales for each year.

STEP 3 — Add a YoY growth column.
  Outside the pivot (next column), for the latest year:
      = (Sales latest year - Sales previous year) / Sales previous year
  Format as percentage.

STEP 4 — Which region grew most? Write the answer to Q2 in a cell.

items.title: Furniture deep-dive
items.body:
STEP 1 — New pivot from Orders.
  Filter: Category = Furniture
  ROWS: Sub-Category
  VALUES: Sum of Profit

STEP 2 — Look at the result.
  YOU SHOULD SEE: Tables loses big money. Bookcases barely break even. Chairs make decent profit. Furnishings make the most.

STEP 3 — Add Region.
  Drag Region to COLUMNS.
  Now you see Furniture profit broken down by region AND sub-category.
  Which region is best for Furniture? Worst?

STEP 4 — Write the answer to Q3.
  Is Furniture overall profitable? (Add all the numbers — what's the total?)
  Where does the profit come from?

days.title: Build the dashboard + write the memo

items.title: Dashboard + Memo + Push
items.body:
STEP 1 — Make a new sheet called 'Dashboard'.

STEP 2 — Top row: 4 KPI cells.
  Total Sales: =SUM(Orders!N:N)
  Total Profit: =SUM(Orders!R:R)
  Profit Margin: =SUM(Orders!R:R) / SUM(Orders!N:N) (format as %)
  YoY Growth (latest year): use the formula from Day 5
  Style: make each cell big — font 20, bold, with a colored border.

STEP 3 — Middle: 2 charts.
  Chart 1: monthly sales trend (line). Source: a small pivot of Sales by month.
  Chart 2: sales by region (bar). Source: pivot of Sales by Region.

STEP 4 — Bottom: top 5 / bottom 5 sub-categories by margin (paste from Day 4 pivot).

STEP 5 — Write the memo.
  Open Word or Google Docs. Make a 1-page document. Use this exact structure:

      # Sample Superstore — Memo to leadership
      
      ## Headline
      (one sentence summarising everything)
      
      ## Q1. Margin leaders & laggards
      Highest margin: [name] at [%]
      Lowest margin: [name] at [%]
      Recommendation: [1 sentence — drop the laggard? double down on the leader?]
      
      ## Q2. Regional growth
      Fastest-growing region: [name] at [%] YoY
      Recommendation: [1 sentence]
      
      ## Q3. Furniture profitability
      Furniture total profit: $[X]
      Where the profit comes from: [Furnishings + Chairs mostly; Tables loses money]
      Recommendation: [1 sentence — discontinue Tables?]
      
      ## What I'd do next
      - [bullet 1]
      - [bullet 2]
      - [bullet 3]

  Export as PDF. Save as superstore-memo.pdf in the project folder.

STEP 6 — Push to GitHub.
  Open the 'create new repository' card. Name: superstore-analysis. Public.
  In your terminal:
      cd Desktop/superstore-analysis
      git init
      git add .
      git commit -m "Sample Superstore analysis v0.1"
      git branch -M main
      git remote add origin https://github.com/YOUR-USERNAME/superstore-analysis.git
      git push -u origin main

STEP 7 — Take a screenshot of the dashboard and add to README.

PASS CRITERIA — Superstore v0.1 ships when:
  ☐ Dashboard sheet with 4 KPIs + 2 charts + 1 table
  ☐ All 3 questions answered with specific numbers
  ☐ 1-page memo exported as PDF
  ☐ Public GitHub repo named superstore-analysis
  ☐ README has dashboard screenshot + link to memo PDF

weeks.title: Superstore v0.2: Discount-vs-Profit deep dive
weeks.context: Last week you answered 3 broad questions. This week dig into ONE: does discounting actually grow profit, or eat it? Build a real scatter + segment table.

items.title: Hypothesis
items.body: Before you look — do you think more discount = more profit, or less? Think: discount drives sales, but it cuts margins. Write your guess.

items.title: Excel/Sheets scatter
items.body:
On the Orders sheet, with all rows visible:
  Select two columns: Discount and Profit.
  Insert → Chart → Scatter (X-Y).
  YOU SHOULD SEE: a cloud of points. Most are clustered around 0% discount with small profits.
  Save as chart in a sheet called Scatter.

items.title: Discount buckets
items.body:
In a helper column on Orders, add 'Discount Bucket':
      =IF(O2=0, "0%", IF(O2<=0.1, "0-10%", IF(O2<=0.2, "10-20%", IF(O2<=0.4, "20-40%", "40%+"))))

Pivot: Rows = Discount Bucket. Values = SUM Profit, COUNT, AVG Discount, AVG Profit.
What pattern do you see? Where does profit go negative?

items.title: Cross-section
items.body:
New pivot. Rows = Category, Columns = Discount Bucket, Values = SUM Profit.
Color-code red where the value is negative.
Which category tolerates discounts? Which is destroyed by them?

items.title: Sweet spot
items.body: Plot a line chart: x = Discount Bucket (in order), y = AVG Profit. Where does the line cross zero? That's the danger zone.

items.title: Memo v2
items.body:
Add a 4th section to your Superstore Memo PDF:
      ## Discount strategy
      Headline: Discounts above XX% destroy profit in [Category Y].
      Recommendation: Cap discounts at XX% for Category Y.
Re-export PDF.

items.title: Acceptance v0.2
items.body:
git add . && git commit -m 'v0.2: discount-profit deep dive'
      git tag v0.2 && git push --tags

PASS:
  ☐ Scatter plot saved
  ☐ Discount bucket pivot built
  ☐ Category × Bucket cross-pivot built
  ☐ Memo PDF v2 includes discount strategy section
  ☐ v0.2 tag

weeks.title: Superstore v0.4: SQL version
weeks.context: Everything you did in pivots can also be done in SQL — the language of every real database. Today you redo the same analysis in SQL.

items.title: SQLite Online — free in-browser SQL
items.why: Click 'Open' to use SQL right in your browser, no install.

items.title: Get Superstore into SQL
items.body:
Export the Orders sheet from Excel as 'orders.csv'.
In sqliteonline.com: Import → CSV → upload orders.csv → create table 'orders'.
Run: SELECT COUNT(*) FROM orders;
YOU SHOULD SEE: about 10,000 rows.

items.title: Margin leaders in SQL
items.body:
SELECT 
        "Sub-Category",
        SUM(Sales) AS total_sales,
        SUM(Profit) AS total_profit,
        SUM(Profit) * 1.0 / SUM(Sales) AS margin
      FROM orders
      GROUP BY "Sub-Category"
      ORDER BY margin DESC;

Save this query in queries.sql. Compare to your pivot — same answer?

items.title: Year-over-year in SQL
items.body:
SELECT 
        Region,
        strftime('%Y', "Order Date") AS year,
        SUM(Sales) AS total_sales
      FROM orders
      GROUP BY Region, year
      ORDER BY Region, year;

Compute YoY growth with a CTE:
      WITH yearly AS (
        SELECT Region, strftime('%Y', "Order Date") AS year, SUM(Sales) AS sales
        FROM orders GROUP BY Region, year
      )
      SELECT a.Region, a.year, a.sales,
             (a.sales - b.sales) * 1.0 / b.sales AS yoy_growth
      FROM yearly a
      LEFT JOIN yearly b ON a.Region = b.Region AND a.year = CAST(b.year AS INT) + 1
      ORDER BY a.Region, a.year;

items.title: Top 10 customers
items.body:
SELECT 
        "Customer ID", "Customer Name",
        SUM(Sales) AS lifetime_sales,
        SUM(Profit) AS lifetime_profit,
        COUNT(DISTINCT "Order ID") AS order_count
      FROM orders
      GROUP BY "Customer ID", "Customer Name"
      ORDER BY lifetime_sales DESC
      LIMIT 10;

items.title: queries.sql
items.body:
Save at least 10 queries in queries.sql, each with a comment explaining what it answers:
  - Total Sales 2023
  - Margin by sub-category
  - YoY growth by region
  - Top 10 customers
  - Discount bucket vs avg profit
  - Furniture profit by sub-category
  - Repeat-buyer rate
  - VIP segmentation
  - Worst single order
  - Average days from order to ship

items.title: Acceptance v0.4
items.body:
git add queries.sql

weeks.title: Data Cleaning
weeks.context: Real-world data is almost never clean. Up to 80\% of an analyst's time is spent cleaning data. This week you develop the discipline and techniques to transform raw, messy data into analysis-ready form.
topics: Identifying and handling missing values: dropna(), fillna(), interpolation
Detecting and removing duplicate rows
Data type conversion and coercion
Outlier detection with IQR and Z-score methods
String cleaning: strip(), lower(), replace(), regex with str.extract()
Date and time parsing: pd.to_datetime(), extracting day/month/year
Column standardisation and renaming conventions
Saving cleaned data back to CSV or Excel
tasks: Download the messy HR / Employee dataset from Kaggle (see resources)
Document all data quality issues you find BEFORE touching any code
Write a step-by-step cleaning notebook that fixes each issue programmatically
Validate the cleaned dataset: zero nulls in critical columns, correct dtypes, no duplicates
Write a data quality report comparing before vs after cleaning
weeks.project: Real-World Cleaning Pipeline — The messy HR dataset contains inconsistent capitalisation, missing salary data, invalid dates, duplicate records, and outlier ages. Clean the entire dataset programmatically (no manual editing), document every decision, and save the clean version. Your code must produce the same result when re-run from scratch.

resources.label: Messy HR / Employee Dataset on Kaggle
Data Cleaning in Pandas — Alex The Analyst
Working with Dates and Times in Pandas — Corey Schafer
Pandas Official Guide: Handling Missing Data
Data Cleaning with Pandas — Real Python

questions: Before cleaning: calculate the average salary in the raw HR dataset. After cleaning: recalculate it. Did the number change? By how much? Identify exactly which rows or values were responsible for the change.
Which department had the most data quality issues (nulls, duplicates, or invalid values combined) in the raw file? What proportion of that department's records needed at least one fix?

After removing outliers from the Age column using the IQR method: how many rows were removed? What was the age range of the removed outliers? Are these plausible data entry errors, or could any of them be real edge cases?

How many employees have a hire date that is impossible or suspicious (e.g., before 1970 or in the future)? These are likely data entry errors. Write out your decision: do you drop them, flag them, or impute them, and why?
exercises: Given a column 'Age' with values like '25', '30 years', 'N/A', '45', '-' — extract numeric values and handle non-numeric entries.
Write a function that detects outliers in any numeric column using the IQR method and returns the outlier rows.
Parse a column of mixed-format dates into a consistent datetime format.
Write a cleaning function that takes a raw DataFrame, returns a cleaned version, and prints a log of every change made.
outputs: Cleaning Jupyter Notebook with every step documented and explained
Cleaned CSV file ready for analysis
Data Quality Report (Markdown or text): before vs after comparison with row/column counts
Reusable outlier detection function saved in a utils.py file

weeks.title: Exploratory Data Analysis (EDA)
weeks.context: EDA is how analysts understand data before drawing conclusions. This week you learn to ask the right questions, find patterns, detect anomalies, and summarise data in a way that tells a story.
topics: The EDA mindset: ask 10 questions first, then code
Univariate analysis: distributions, histograms, value counts
Bivariate analysis: scatter plots, box plots, cross-tabulations
Correlation analysis: Pearson/Spearman, heatmaps
Grouped analysis: groupby, aggregations, pivot tables in Pandas
Time-based analysis: resampling, rolling averages
Detecting skewness, kurtosis, and data imbalance

Write 10 analytical questions about the dataset BEFORE writing any code
Answer each question with code and a brief written explanation
Build a correlation heatmap and interpret 3 key relationships
Identify the 3 most important findings and write them as insights with business implications
weeks.project: End-to-End EDA Report — Using the Titanic dataset, complete structured EDA: (1) Data overview and missing values, (2) Survival rate by gender, class, and age group, (3) Fare distribution analysis, (4) Correlation heatmap with interpretation, (5) 5 written insights. Present as a clean Jupyter Notebook that reads like a report, not just code.

resources.label: Exploratory Data Analysis with Pandas — Alex The Analyst
Seaborn Chart Gallery
resources.note: (browse for chart ideas — click any chart for its code)

questions: What is the overall survival rate in the Titanic dataset? Now calculate it separately for male and female passengers. What is the exact percentage point difference between male and female survival rates? If you had to explain this gap to a journalist in one sentence, what would you write?

Calculate the survival rate for each passenger class (1st, 2nd, 3rd). What is the gap between 1st class and 3rd class survival rate? Can the data alone prove this was intentional discrimination, or could other factors explain it?

Bin passengers into age groups: 0—12 (children), 13—18 (teens), 19—35 (young adults), 36—60 (adults), 60+ (elderly). Which age group had the highest survival rate? Which the lowest? Does this match the 'women and children first' narrative?

Among passengers who survived, what was the average fare paid? Compare this to non-survivors. Calculate the ratio. Now ask: does this prove wealth saved lives, or could fare simply be a proxy for passenger class (which also correlated with survival)?

How many passengers have a missing Age value? What percentage is this? If you filled all missing ages with the median age, how would your age-group survival analysis change? Try it and compare the two results.

Write code that automatically flags any numeric column with skewness above 1 and prints a warning.

weeks.title: Statistics for Data Analysis
weeks.context: An analyst without statistical knowledge will draw wrong conclusions. This week you build statistical intuition and practical skills — not abstract theory, but the exact stats used every week on the job.
topics: Descriptive statistics: mean, median, mode, variance, standard deviation
Probability distributions: normal, binomial, Poisson (conceptual intuition)
Central Limit Theorem and its implications for analysis
Hypothesis testing: null hypothesis, p-value, significance level (alpha)
t-test: one-sample, two-sample, paired
Chi-square test for categorical data
Confidence intervals
A/B testing fundamentals
tasks: Watch ALL StatQuest videos in the resource list (required before any code)
Use scipy.stats to run a two-sample t-test on a real dataset
Run a chi-square test on categorical data (gender vs survival in Titanic)
Design a simple A/B test scenario for a fictional e-commerce site
Write a 1-page explanation of p-values that a non-technical manager could understand
weeks.project: Statistical Audit — Using the Titanic dataset, test: (1) Is there a statistically significant difference in survival rates between male and female passengers? (2) Is there a significant relationship between ticket class and survival? (3) Is the average fare for survivors significantly different from non-survivors? Document your hypothesis, test used, p-value, and conclusion for each.

resources.label: StatQuest with Josh Starmer — YouTube Channel
resources.note: (subscribe and watch the Statistics Fundamentals playlist)

resources.label: scipy.stats Documentation
resources.note: (reference for running t-tests and chi-square in Python)

questions: Run a chi-square test on gender (Sex) vs survival (Survived) in the Titanic dataset. State your null hypothesis. Report the chi-square statistic and p-value. At the 95\% confidence level, can you reject the null? Write your conclusion in one plain-English sentence a manager could understand.

Run an independent-samples t-test comparing the average Fare paid by survivors vs non-survivors. Is the difference statistically significant at p < 0.05? What would it mean if the p-value were 0.4 instead? Would you still report the difference?
Calculate a 95\% confidence interval for the mean age of all Titanic passengers. Interpret it correctly: what does it mean to say you are 95\% confident the true mean falls in this range?

questions: You have just completed 18 weeks of work. Your Week 1 self used Excel and did not know what a DataFrame was. Name one specific thing you believed about data analysis in Week 1 that you now know is wrong or oversimplified. Describe exactly what changed in your understanding.

Take your most important capstone finding and express it in exactly one sentence that a non-analyst could act on. Now ask someone outside this programme to read it. Did they immediately understand what action to take? If not, rewrite it until they do.

Identify the single weakest part of your capstone analysis — be brutally specific. Not 'I could have used more data' but something like: 'I did not control for [X], which means my finding on [Y] could alternatively be explained by [Z].' Write this as the 'Limitations' section of your report.

If a real organisation in The Gambia or West Africa implemented the main recommendation from your capstone: what would success look like in 12 months? How would you measure it? What data would you collect to know if the recommendation worked?
